title: A ten-year budget and Weibull failure risk

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: An analyst values a 2031 replacement with the unit's 2027 PoF times its CoF, the first lesson's coefficient. What does the page say that coefficient leaves out?

options.text: Nothing, since the PoF column already covers every plan year
options.says: The column is one number per unit, for 2027; the plan needs one per year.

options.text: Only the discount, since a kept unit's PoF stays level each year
options.says: T00076's PoF rises from 0.082 in 2027 to 0.107 in 2036.

options.text: The aging of the kept unit, and the new unit's own failure curve
options.says: Right: the old unit ages while it waits, and the new one starts its own curve.

options.text: The CoF by year, since the PoF column is already given per year
options.says: The PoF column holds one value per unit, for 2027 only.

origin.section: One Year's PoF Cannot Value a Plan That Waits

questions.stem: A planner sets the risk window equal to the plan's ten years, 2027 to 2036. What happens to the value of a replacement in 2036?

options.text: It counts one year of benefit, so it looks nearly worthless
options.says: Right: T00076's 2036 coefficient falls to 8% of its 2027 one with ten years.

options.text: It counts ten years of benefit, the same as a 2027 one
options.says: With a ten-year window a 2036 start counts only 2036.

options.text: It counts nothing, since benefit after 2027 is discounted away
options.says: Discounting shrinks later years; T00076's 2036 coefficient is still 411.

options.text: It counts more, since a later start removes more risk per year
options.says: Every coefficient falls with a later start.

origin.section: A Replacement's Value Is the Risk It Removes Over a Window, Discounted

questions.stem: A test asks the old one-year code whether replacing A in 2027 and B in 2028 is allowed: two $600k units, $1,000k a year. Why does the old code refuse it?

options.text: Its curve stub returns 0, so A and B have no value to allow
options.says: `feasible` reads no coefficient, so a curve that returns 0 cannot make a list infeasible.

options.text: Its age screen drops A and B, so neither one can be replaced
options.says: The old model ignores `min_age`, so it screens out no unit.

options.text: Its gap stops the solve before it can place A and B at all
options.says: The old model ignores `gap`, so it stops no solve early.

options.text: It keeps one variable per unit, so A and B fall in one year
options.says: Right: one variable per unit, so both are fixed to 1 in the one year, $1,200k against $1,000k.

origin.section: The Tests Pin the Curve, the Timing and Each Year's Row
